clinicalPearls: Acanthocephaliasis is a rare intestinal infection by thorny-headed worms, chiefly Macracanthorhynchus hirudinaceus and Moniliformis moniliformis
Humans are accidental hosts, infected by eating raw or undercooked arthropod intermediate hosts such as beetles, cockroaches or other insects
The worm's defining feature is a retractable proboscis armed with hooks that anchors into the intestinal wall
Many infections are asymptomatic or cause mild abdominal pain, whereas heavy infection can produce more marked gastrointestinal symptoms
Deep attachment of the proboscis can cause focal inflammation, ulceration and, rarely, bowel perforation with peritonitis
Diagnosis relies on identifying characteristic eggs in stool or recovering an expelled or endoscopically visualised worm
Management is with antihelminthic therapy, and surgery is reserved for perforation or other complications
reference.pathophysiology: Infection is acquired when a person ingests an arthropod harbouring the larval (cystacanth) stage of an acanthocephalan. In the intestine the larva develops into an adult worm that lacks a digestive tract and absorbs nutrients across its surface. Its hallmark is a spiny, retractable proboscis that embeds into the intestinal mucosa, provoking localised inflammation and, with deeper penetration, ulceration or full-thickness injury. Most damage is therefore mechanical and focal at the attachment site; systemic disease is uncommon and severe complications such as perforation are rare.
additionalDifferentials: Other intestinal helminth infections such as ascariasis or trichuriasis
Appendicitis or other causes of an acute abdomen when perforation occurs
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for characteristic acanthocephalan eggs
Morphological identification of any expelled or extracted worm
Endoscopy to visualise and retrieve attached worms
Abdominal imaging if perforation or complication is suspected
Full blood count including eosinophil assessment
Detailed dietary and exposure history for ingestion of insects or arthropods
redFlags: Signs of peritonitis suggesting intestinal perforation
Severe or persistent abdominal pain with systemic features
Heavy worm burden with marked symptoms
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent in most cases, as infection is usually mild and self-limited or readily treated; the rare complication of perforation carries the morbidity of any acute abdomen but is uncommon.
pitfalls: Failing to consider the diagnosis because of its rarity
Not taking a dietary history for ingestion of insects or arthropods
Misidentifying eggs or worms without expert parasitological input
Overlooking perforation as a cause of acute abdominal deterioration
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with anthelmintic therapy, using a benzimidazole such as albendazole or mebendazole, with pyrantel pamoate as an alternative, to eradicate the worm
Remove an accessible attached worm endoscopically, which can be both diagnostic and therapeutic
Provide supportive care and analgesia for abdominal symptoms and ensure adequate hydration
Manage the rare complication of bowel perforation or peritonitis surgically as an acute abdomen
Confirm clearance with follow-up stool examination after treatment
Prevent reinfection through food hygiene and by avoiding ingestion of raw or undercooked arthropods such as beetles and cockroaches
